faq.a: Yes, especially when patients are on anticoagulation; however, bleeding is rare without anticoagulant therapy.
They are related but distinct; anticardiolipin antibodies are another antiphospholipid antibody, often present together with LA.
faq.q: Is lupus anticoagulant the same as anticardiolipin antibody?

faq.a: A prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing is a practical surrogate when dRVVT is unavailable.
faq.q: What is the best test for LA in a low‑resource setting?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with a history of two spontaneous abortions presents with a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the most appropriate anticoagulant? — Warfarin, target INR 2–3, because LA interferes with aPTT monitoring of heparin.
A patient on warfarin has a sudden drop in INR to 1.2. What is the likely cause? — Possible lupus anticoagulant causing prolonged aPTT and unreliable INR measurement.
A 35‑year‑old man with HIV presents with a prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing. What is the diagnosis? — Likely factor deficiency (e.g., hemophilia) rather than LA.
A patient with confirmed LA develops a pulmonary embolism. What is the first step in management? — Initiate therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin and maintain INR 2–3.

A pregnant woman with LA is on low‑dose aspirin. She develops a spontaneous abortion. What should be added? — Therapeutic warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy; consider low‑dose heparin with target aPTT 1.5–2.5× control.
A patient with LA has a normal dRVVT but a prolonged aPTT. What explains this? — The dRVVT reagent may have insufficient phospholipid; repeat with a phospholipid‑rich reagent.
ai.title: Lupus Anticoagulant
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A lupus anticoagulant is an antiphospholipid antibody that paradoxically prolongs clotting tests in vitro but promotes thrombosis in vivo. It is a key marker of antiphospholipid syndrome and requires careful interpretation in low‑resource settings.

b: LA is not a clotting factor; it is an inhibitor of in vitro coagulation but a pro‑thrombotic factor in vivo.
sections.p: Lupus anticoagulant (LA) is a circulating IgG/IgM antibody that binds phospholipid‑protein complexes, interfering with phospholipid‑dependent coagulation assays. Diagnosis requires a prolonged aPTT that does not correct with mixing, confirmed on two separate occasions 12 weeks apart.

b: Asymptomatic seropositivity requires no treatment but close monitoring.
sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical phenotype: thrombosis (arterial or venous), pregnancy morbidity, or asymptomatic seropositivity. Staging follows the Sydney criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome: one clinical and one laboratory criterion.

b: In low‑resource settings, treat underlying infection first; LA may resolve with infection control.
sections.p: Primary antiphospholipid syndrome is idiopathic. Secondary causes include infections (HIV, TB, malaria), autoimmune diseases (SLE), malignancy, and certain drugs (e.g., oral contraceptives). In East Africa, HIV and malaria are common triggers.

b: Typical presentation: deep vein thrombosis in a young woman with a history of miscarriages.
sections.p: Patients present with unexplained venous or arterial thrombosis, recurrent miscarriages, or livedo reticularis. Bleeding is uncommon but can occur with anticoagulation.

b: If dRVVT unavailable, a prolonged aPTT with no correction on mixing is a reasonable surrogate.
sections.p: Key tests are aPTT, dilute Russell viper venom time (dRVVT), and mixing studies. Repeat testing 12 weeks apart confirms persistence.

t.b: Does the patient have a prolonged clotting time? A prolonged aPTT that does not correct with 1:1 mixing suggests an inhibitor like LA.
Is the clotting time prolonged after adding phospholipid? A prolonged dRVVT that corrects with excess phospholipid is typical of LA.
Does adding normal plasma correct the aPTT? No correction indicates an inhibitor.
Is the abnormality persistent? Persistence confirms LA diagnosis.

b: Urgent anticoagulation is required if a new thrombus is suspected.
sections.p: Thrombosis (DVT, PE, stroke), pregnancy loss, livedo reticularis, and catastrophic APS (rapid multi‑organ failure).

b: Warfarin is preferred over LMWH in chronic management because it is cheaper and easier to monitor in low‑resource settings.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Anticoagulation with warfarin (target INR 2–3) is standard for thrombosis; low‑dose aspirin for pregnancy morbidity. Avoid heparin if LA is present due to unreliable aPTT monitoring.

b: Patients with LA should avoid estrogen‑containing contraceptives.
sections.p: Regular monitoring of INR, repeat LA testing every 6–12 months, and patient education on signs of thrombosis. In pregnancy, maintain therapeutic INR and consider low‑dose aspirin.

b: A prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing rules out LA.
sections.p: Coagulation factor deficiencies (e.g., hemophilia), heparin therapy, and vitamin K deficiency all prolong aPTT but correct on mixing.

b: In low‑resource labs, a normal aPTT does not exclude LA if the test is not performed with adequate phospholipid.
sections.p: aPTT can be falsely prolonged by lupus anticoagulant but may be normal if the assay uses low phospholipid concentration. dRVVT may be falsely normal if the reagent is deficient in phospholipid.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden limb swelling or pain suggesting DVT
Severe abdominal pain with suspected mesenteric thrombosis
